title: Prune Twin Folder Trees
statement:
A file system is given as a list of folder paths. paths[i] is one folder, written as the list of folder names from the top level down, so ["docs", "img"] is the folder /docs/img. Every parent of a listed folder is listed too, and no path appears twice.

Call two folders twins when they hold the same non-empty set of subfolders, with the same names and the same structure all the way down. The two folders' own names do not matter, and they may sit at different depths. Empty folders are never twins.

Mark every folder that has at least one twin. Then delete every marked folder together with everything inside it. Deletion happens once: folders that only look alike after the deletion stay.

Return the paths of the remaining folders, in any order.

examples.why: /x and /y each hold exactly one empty folder named m, so they are twins and both go, together with their m folders.
/p and /s differ (only /s has t), but /p/q and /s/q both hold just r. Those two are twins and are deleted with their contents.
/a/p and /c both hold just m and are deleted. /a and /b now look the same, but they were not twins before the deletion, so they stay.

constraints: Total number of names over all paths ≤ 200 000
Every parent of a listed folder is also listed; all paths are distinct
hints: Build the folder tree first: a trie where each node maps a child name to a child node.
Two folders are twins when their subtrees look the same. Can you turn each subtree into a single string, so that equal structures give equal strings?

Serialise bottom-up with the children sorted by name, for example name(childSig) joined in order. Count each non-empty signature; then walk the tree again and skip any node whose signature was seen at least twice.

explain.intuition:
Comparing every pair of folders structure by structure is far too slow. Instead give every folder a fingerprint: a string that describes what is inside it, built bottom-up. A folder's fingerprint is the list of its children, sorted by name, each written as name(fingerprint of that child). Two folders have equal fingerprints exactly when their contents are identical, and the folder's own name is not part of its own fingerprint, so twins at different depths match.

Then it is just counting. Put every non-empty fingerprint into a hash map with a count. A second walk from the top skips any folder whose fingerprint occurs twice or more, which also drops its whole subtree. This is how a virtual DOM can spot identical subtrees: hash children bottom-up, compare hashes, not trees.
steps: Insert every path into a trie. Each node keeps a map from child name to child node.
Post-order DFS: compute each node's signature from its children in sorted name order, as name(sig) pieces joined together. Store it on the node.
Count every non-empty signature in a hash map.
DFS again from the root, building the current path. Skip a child whose signature is non-empty and counted at least twice; otherwise record its path and continue into it.
pitfalls: Treating empty folders as twins. Two leaves have the same empty signature, but the rules say only non-empty folders can be twins.
Forgetting to sort children by name. The input order of paths is arbitrary, so the same structure could produce two different strings.
Deleting repeatedly. After the first deletion, new look-alikes may appear (example 3); they must stay.

complexity.time: O(L · log k) for L total names and up to k children per folder, plus the signature lengths

solutions.title: Compare every pair of folders
solutions.idea: Build the trie, then compare every pair of non-empty folders structurally. Mark both when they match.

solutions.title: Trie + subtree signatures
solutions.idea: Give each folder a canonical string of its contents, bottom-up with sorted children. Count signatures, then skip folders whose signature repeats.
solutions.time: O(L log k + total signature length)

followups: The signatures can get long for deep trees. How would you replace each one with a small integer id so comparisons stay O(1)?
Keep deleting until no twins remain. What changes, and how many rounds can it take?
